chapters.title: Chapter 1774 The Primordial Villain
paragraphs: The three-story buildings alone would have been extraordinary in any settlement on the continent, where commoners lived in single-story hovels and minor nobles rarely built above two.
Here, every building had three heated floors with quartz windows, and the city stayed open and walkable despite housing a hundred thousand people.
Old-growth trees rose from gaps in the road where any other builder would have laid more stone.
Myrasyn ran her fingers along an oak trunk as they passed, and beneath her hood, her ears twitched. "Outstanding... This tree... Despite having just been built around... It's happy. So happy..."
Alexios was quiet for several minutes.
A mage who could raise a city like this in an afternoon would transform any kingdom.
His eyes drifted to Morgana.
She'd commanded the same seven elements for centuries, buried in her research the entire time, and it had never occurred to her to build a single wall.
Even if she couldn't replicate the sheer scale, or make the magma chamber... Those were luxuries people could manage without.
But buildings made of reinforced earth?
His border settlements near the beastkin raids, the ones his soldiers rebuilt by hand every few years, could have looked similar to this if she tried.
The look he gave his wife lasted two seconds, and the disappointment in it carried centuries of squandered potential. Morgana caught all of it.
Her chin rose, and the arrogance in her iridescent eyes came from knowing he wasn't wrong.
"A waste of time."
"..." the disappointment in her husband's expression grew to new heights as he didn't even try to argue, knowing it was futile.
"Hahaha! It's winter but I don't even need boots! So fun!"
A shriek cut through the street.

A girl of nine or ten years came tearing around the corner, barefoot and laughing, a half-open bucket of bright yellow paint clutched to her chest. She was running so fast she didn't see the group until she was among them, and her foot caught a loose stone and sent her sprawling.
The bucket went up.
Yellow paint hit Quinlan's chest in a wide, spectacular splash.
"Ow...!" The girl curled around her foot, tears springing to her eyes.
The spot where she'd kicked the stone was already swelling red. Then she panicked, looking up with a frightened expression. "I-I'm sorry! I'm so sorry, I didn't-!"
Quinlan looked down at his paint-covered shirt.
"Wait!" Elisabeth's hand shot forward. "Villain, don't hurt-!"
Out of all people, it was Alexios who grabbed his daughter's shoulder.
"What?!" she shouted, but he merely shook his head. "Let me go, he will-"
Alexios shook his head.

He understood the anomalous man well enough to know the girl was in no danger, and watched with a mind that housed a myriad of difficult thoughts as Quinlan crouched beside the girl, caught her under the arms, and set her on her feet.
"Huh? Mister?"
She yelped, shocked, and stared up at him with wet eyes, waiting for the anger that was supposed to follow.
He brushed the grit from her knees, and she just stood there, sniffling, watching his hands work like she couldn't understand why they were being gentle.
"Hmm..." Quinlan looked at her foot. "Does it hurt badly?"
"Y-yes... Very..." the girl nodded, even if she was thoroughly confused.
"Let's see..." He produced a crystal vial and uncorked it with his thumb, pouring a thin stream over the swelling, and the redness faded before she could finish flinching.
The girl gasped. She wiggled her toes, looked down at her foot, wiggled them again. "It doesn't hurt anymore...! How'd you do that?!"
"A healing potion, my wife made it."

"A healing potion?!" The girl's expression turned from wonder to horror in a heartbeat. Her bottom lip started trembling and her voice came out so small it barely carried. "B-but Papa says those cost more money than he makes in a whole month... We can't... I can't pay you back..."
Her breathing quickened, eyes darting between the vial and Quinlan's face, and she looked seconds away from a full meltdown.
"My wife makes a lot of these." Quinlan's voice was easy and warm. "She'd kill me if I charged your father for it."
The girl froze mid-panic. "...Really?"
"Really."
Her eyes brightened so fast it was like watching a candle get lit. "Your wife sounds wonderful! Is she pretty?"
"The prettiest."
The girl beamed at him, all traces of terror gone, replaced by the unshakeable conviction that any man with a pretty wife who made free healing potions had to be a good person.
"Take the rest home." He pressed the vial into her small hands. "Pour more on it if it still hurts later."
She looked at the vial, then at him, then back at the vial.
Her fingers closed around it slowly, carefully, and she pulled it to her chest with both hands, holding it so tight she might as well have been cradling a baby bird.
Then Quinlan's eyes drifted to the ground, where most of the yellow paint had splattered across the warm stone in a wide, ruined puddle.
Too much dirt and grit mixed in to save.
The girl followed his gaze.
Her shoulders drooped and her grip on the vial loosened as the joy drained right back out of her, bracing for the scolding she knew she'd receive back home.
Quinlan smiled at that, then fished a handful of silver coins from his pocket and pressed them into her other hand. "Here, tell your parents my carelessness caused this, so I paid for it."
She stared at the coins, then at the vial she was already holding, then back at the coins, and her mouth opened and closed several times without producing a single word.
Then, finally... "Thank you..."
"Don't mention it."
The girl nodded, then tilted her head and squinted at him. "W-why are you all dirty, mister? You're dressed like... the rest of us?"
"So my cover was blown, huh?" He grinned and tilted his head toward the group behind him. "Showing my friends around."

Her eyes snapped open, wide like saucers. "The builder man is showing friends around!! Everyone has to-" Her gaze began frantically darting round, a breath away from shouting something that would've ended every disguise in the procession, and Quinlan pressed a finger to his lips.
"It's no fun if everyone pretends to behave."
She gaped at him, snapped her mouth shut, and nodded so hard her entire body bounced.
"Get going now. And just because the ground is nice and warm to run on doesn't mean you shouldn't watch where you step."
"O-okay!!" she shouted excitedly then immediately yelped, realizing she was blowing their cover.

"I'm sorry!! I'll behave now!" Then she clutched the vial and the coins tighter and bolted down the street because she had been trusted with the biggest secret of her life and she was not going to ruin it.
Elisabeth hadn't moved.

She stood where she'd lunged, hand still half-raised, watching the girl disappear around the corner with the vial and coins the Primordial Villain had pressed into her hands, and for the first time all day the Arch Priestess had nothing to say.
What she'd just watched didn't fit inside the world she'd built for herself, and she wasn't ready to think about why.
"The Primordial Villain...?" the words left her lips without meaning to.
"The big bad evil..." two turbo smug elven ladies grinned at the priestess. "You must eradicate him or the world will end..."
"S-shut it!" Elisabeth hissed, cheeks going pink.
The procession began moving again soon and then rounded a bend in the road.
A wide square opened before them, cobbled in the same heated stone, with market stalls lining the edges and a modest cathedral rising at the far end.

It was unmistakable. The spire bore the Goddess's sigil, the same golden sunburst that hung above every church on the continent, and the doors were open wide with warm light spilling out into the square.
Elisabeth's breath hitched. "That's..."

The Arch Priestess stared at the cathedral with a storm of emotions crashing behind her golden eyes, because a Goddess church standing openly in the Primordial Villain's city was an impossibility her heart hadn't prepared for, even after being told of its existence.
But then her gaze drifted sideways, away from the cathedral, across the square to the far end of the market where the stalls thinned out near a residential street.

A woman in white priestess robes stood at a fabric stall with her sleeves pushed up to her elbows, holding a bolt of linen up to the light while chatting with the housewife beside her as if they'd known each other for years.
"He did that?" the woman in white gasped.
"I know, right?! It's outrageous!" the housewife was furious. "I ought to put laxatives in his dinner. Hmph!"
"No, I wouldn't go that far... Just maybe..."
"Don't satisfy him in bed?"
"...I didn't say that."
"But you thought of it!"
No guards flanked her, no escort trailed behind, no ceremonial staff rested against the stall.
She was hundreds of meters from the cathedral, completely alone, chattering with the housewife while the merchant waited patiently for them to finish gossiping with a tired expression.
Elisabeth's face went white.
"...Arch Priestess Velara?!"

"A healing potion, my wife made it."
"A healing potion?!" The girl's expression turned from wonder to horror in a heartbeat.
Her bottom lip started trembling and her voice came out so small it barely carried.
"B-but Papa says those cost more money than he makes in a whole month...
We can't...
I can't pay you back..."
Her breathing quickened, eyes darting between the vial and Quinlan's face, and she looked seconds away from a full meltdown.
"My wife makes a lot of these." Quinlan's voice was easy and warm.
"She'd kill me if I charged your father for it."
The girl froze mid-panic.
"...Really?"
"Really."
Her eyes brightened so fast it was like watching a candle get lit.
"Your wife sounds wonderful!
Is she pretty?"
"The prettiest."
The girl beamed at him, all traces of terror gone, replaced by the unshakeable conviction that any man with a pretty wife who made free healing potions had to be a good person.
"Take the rest home." He pressed the vial into her small hands.
"Pour more on it if it still hurts later."
She looked at the vial, then at him, then back at the vial.
Her fingers closed around it slowly, carefully, and she pulled it to her chest with both hands, holding it so tight she might as well have been cradling a baby bird.
Then Quinlan's eyes drifted to the ground, where most of the yellow paint had splattered across the warm stone in a wide, ruined puddle.
Too much dirt and grit mixed in to save.
The girl followed his gaze.
Her shoulders drooped and her grip on the vial loosened as the joy drained right back out of her, bracing for the scolding she knew she'd receive back home.
Quinlan smiled at that, then fished a handful of silver coins from his pocket and pressed them into her other hand.
"Here, tell your parents my carelessness caused this, so I paid for it."
She stared at the coins, then at the vial she was already holding, then back at the coins, and her mouth opened and closed several times without producing a single word.
Then, finally...
"Thank you..."
"Don't mention it."
The girl nodded, then tilted her head and squinted at him.
"W-why are you all dirty, mister?
You're dressed like... the rest of us?"
"So my cover was blown, huh?" He grinned and tilted his head toward the group behind him.
"Showing my friends around."
Her eyes snapped open, wide like saucers.
"The builder man is showing friends around!!
Everyone has to-" Her gaze began frantically darting round, a breath away from shouting something that would've ended every disguise in the procession, and Quinlan pressed a finger to his lips.
"It's no fun if everyone pretends to behave."
She gaped at him, snapped her mouth shut, and nodded so hard her entire body bounced.
"Get going now.
And just because the ground is nice and warm to run on doesn't mean you shouldn't watch where you step."
"O-okay!!" she shouted excitedly then immediately yelped, realizing she was blowing their cover.
"I'm sorry!!
I'll behave now!" Then she clutched the vial and the coins tighter and bolted down the street because she had been trusted with the biggest secret of her life and she was not going to ruin it.
Elisabeth hadn't moved.

She stood where she'd lunged, hand still half-raised, watching the girl disappear around the corner with the vial and coins the Primordial Villain had pressed into her hands, and for the first time all day the Arch Priestess had nothing to say.
What she'd just watched didn't fit inside the world she'd built for herself, and she wasn't ready to think about why.
"The Primordial Villain...?" the words left her lips without meaning to.
"The big bad evil..." two turbo smug elven ladies grinned at the priestess.
"You must eradicate him or the world will end..."
"S-shut it!" Elisabeth hissed, cheeks going pink.
The procession began moving again soon and then rounded a bend in the road.
A wide square opened before them, cobbled in the same heated stone, with market stalls lining the edges and a modest cathedral rising at the far end.
It was unmistakable.
The spire bore the Goddess's sigil, the same golden sunburst that hung above every church on the continent, and the doors were open wide with warm light spilling out into the square.
Elisabeth's breath hitched.
"That's..."

The Arch Priestess stared at the cathedral with a storm of emotions crashing behind her golden eyes, because a Goddess church standing openly in the Primordial Villain's city was an impossibility her heart hadn't prepared for, even after being told of its existence.
But then her gaze drifted sideways, away from the cathedral, across the square to the far end of the market where the stalls thinned out near a residential street.

A woman in white priestess robes stood at a fabric stall with her sleeves pushed up to her elbows, holding a bolt of linen up to the light while chatting with the housewife beside her as if they'd known each other for years.
"He did that?" the woman in white gasped.
"I know, right?!
It's outrageous!" the housewife was furious.
"I ought to put laxatives in his dinner.
Hmph!"
"No, I wouldn't go that far...
Just maybe..."
"Don't satisfy him in bed?"
"...I didn't say that."
"But you thought of it!"
No guards flanked her, no escort trailed behind, no ceremonial staff rested against the stall.
She was hundreds of meters from the cathedral, completely alone, chattering with the housewife while the merchant waited patiently for them to finish gossiping with a tired expression.
Elisabeth's face went white.
"...Arch Priestess Velara?!"

chapters.title: Chapter 1775 Inside a Holy Sanctuary
paragraphs: Elisabeth's face went white.
"...Arch Priestess Velara?!"
Velara's fingers were mid-count on a handful of copper when Elisabeth's voice hit her.
"Wha-"

Her head came up. A woman in commoner wool was staring at her from across the square, golden hair spilling from beneath a rough hood, and it took Velara two squinting seconds before the face beneath it registered.
"E-Elisabeth...?"
Then her gaze traversed the rest of the group as if pulled by gravity until it reached the tall figure at its center, and the laborer's tunic did absolutely nothing to help.
Truth be told, while the maids and the robes tried their best to let them blend in, their disguises were never meant to survive a direct stare from people who knew them well.
They were just meant to help get a genuine look at the city without turning every head.
If Quinlan wanted to hide him and his guests better, he could have.
But showing off his amazing maids was part of the tour. He wouldn't have it any other way.
Velara's eyes went wide, and the coin slipped from her fingers.
"Ah!"
She reached for it, caught it between her thumb and forefinger, and it slipped free again.

She grabbed with both hands cupped, missed, lunged as it bounced off the heated cobblestones, and by the time it rolled beneath the fabric stall she was bent at the waist with her face three shades past crimson and the merchant watching her with flat eyes trying their best not to show any emotion.
She was their city's beloved Arch Priestess, after all.
"..." Velara left the coin where it was, visibly coming to the conclusion that a woman of her station crawling under stalls could simply not stand.
Instead, she crossed the distance to Elisabeth in four long strides, and began dragging the Dawn Breaker by the hand.
"Inside," she hissed, herding the entire group toward the cathedral's side entrance with the frantic energy of someone stuffing contraband into a cupboard. "Now. All of you. Move."
Elisabeth stopped dead the moment she crossed the threshold. "You're inviting him into a cathedral?!" She jabbed a finger at Quinlan.
"Well, he built it..." Velara sighed at the fuming priestess while she took a proper look at her visitors in the light.
She stared at Elisabeth first. "Wait, why in the Goddess's name are you dressed like a milkmaid?"
"Stop changing topics. And this is a vagabond's attire!" Elisabeth corrected, tugging at her roughspun. "Not a milkmaid's."
"You look like a milkmaid," Velara said.
"I do not. The maid who dressed me swore upon the Goddess that she'd make me appear as mighty as possible."
Velara couldn't help but release a weary exhale. "The Goddess's name means nothing to those heretics. She played you."
Then her eyes found Quinlan, expression beyond dry as she added, "Next time you want to ensure that the Villain's allies are truthful, have them swear upon his life."
"How have you been, priestess?" Quinlan smiled at her, as if he hadn't heard a single word of their loud exchange.
"...Been better."
"You seemed to be enjoying yourself a minute ago." His tone was infuriatingly casual.
Velara's eyes narrowed with scrutiny, but the blush rising from her collar gave her away.
She had indeed been enjoying herself and the fact that he'd seen all of that... She didn't like it. Not one bit.
"What happened in the past is inconsequential since after that you showed up, so..." she said flatly.
"Ouch."
"...Huh? Wait!" Elisabeth's head snapped toward Quinlan. "Villain. Explain yourself. The maid said I look mighty even in this outfit."
Quinlan shrugged. "My dutiful maids would never lie. You're the mightiest milkmaid of them all."
Golden light crackled between Elisabeth's fingers, and the Arch Priestess looked ready to commit murder.
"Please refrain from acts of violence in this house of worship," Quinlan murmured, raising a palm. His composure was impeccable. His sincerity was not.
Velara stared at him.

She stared with every drop of patience her centuries of service had earned her, because this man and that lunatic Black Fang had happily attacked her on the steps of her own cathedral, and he was now standing in its replacement preaching the sanctity of holy ground.
She closed her eyes, exhaled through her nose, and accepted that holding the Primordial Villain accountable for his actions or having him admit that he was in the wrong was a war no one could win.
Her gaze moved to the other male instead, and the color left her face all over again.
The roughspun disguise covered everything except the fact that he was the King of Vraven.
"Y-Your Majesty...?!"
"Arch Priestess." Alexios nodded in greeting.

Elisabeth managed to calm herself just enough to rejoin the conversation. "That can wait! Why were you that far from the cathedral?! That stall was hundreds of meters away! Where are your guards? You're an Arch Priestess walking a public market without a single escort!"
"..." Velara straightened her robes and smoothed her hair, and the careful way she did both said more about how rattled she was than the coin fumble had.

She did not look at Quinlan as she answered. "The city is in the middle of settling a hundred thousand displaced people. My guards are more useful carrying crates and directing families than standing behind me while I browse linen."
"You can't be unguarded this far from consecrated ground!" Elisabeth refused to relent. "What if someone gets an idea? They don't even have proper patrols in place yet!"
"Even with loose patrols," Velara said, and the reluctance behind the words cost her visibly, "the city is very safe. Safer than old Whisperfield."
Elisabeth looked at her as if she'd sprouted a second head. "Safer?!" She gestured toward the cathedral's open doors with both hands. "Than Whisperfield?!"
Velara's gaze finally moved to Quinlan, her expression sharpening.

"These people watched this infuriatingly arrogant creature raise their homes from the earth in just a couple of hours," she said, her tone carrying more exasperation than awe. "No one dares take advantage of the chaos, because they are all convinced he would somehow find them and make them pay. They don't understand his capabilities, so they assume the worst."
Elisabeth blinked rapidly and turned to look at the man Velara had just described.
He was no longer listening.
Quinlan had drifted deeper into the cathedral with Jasmine's hand in his, the two of them wandering between stone columns as if continental politics was happening to someone else.
Jasmine was studying the vaulted ceiling with her head tilted, one finger tapping her chin. "You did good with this one, Quin."
"I just gave them walls and a roof. They did the rest."
"The hypocrite's fanatics are truly hard workers."

"They ransacked the old cathedral and brought the decorations over. Then the priestess did her thing and brought the Goddess's presence over. Or something like that. I don't know, for some reason they don't like sharing details with me."
"I wonder why~" Jasmine purred, then added, "I know all that, but it's still impressive to have set up a new church so soon."
"Is that so?"

Jasmine giggled and turned to face him, poking the tip of his nose with her finger. "You know, the fact that we, the girls, did everything when it came to our home's interior decor shows how little you know about making things pretty, Quin."
"I did decorate the sex dungeon in the basement, though? Ronan and I wracked our brains hard on that one."
"Shhh! We have an audience!"
He chuckled, caught her hand before it left his face, and pulled her back to his side.

"Hey, Quin, did you know..." Jasmine hummed, already pivoting to how the cathedral's foot traffic could anchor the surrounding blocks, what the side chambers could host, whether the district heads could hold their meetings here.
Quinlan listened with quiet contentment while his hand slid from hers to the small of her back, then lower, fingers settling on the curve of her butt and kneading slow, idle circles while she talked.
Jasmine rose onto her toes without missing a syllable, her back arching into his side to give his palm better purchase on her behind, and she didn't seem to notice the hand was there.
Or if she did, she was enjoying it too much to care.
Myrasyn and Isveth stood shoulder to shoulder with hoods low, both scandalized by the display and both unable to look anywhere else.

chapters.title: Chapter 1776 Zero Shame
paragraphs: Myrasyn's ears twitched beneath her hood while Isveth kept her eyes peeled, taking all the mannerisms of the Holy Son in without judgment.
Felicity watched the couple from where she stood, smiling, completely unbothered by the public groping happening in front of her.
Alexios looked at his daughter. Then at the Villain's hand openly kneading his woman's rear inside a cathedral. Then back at his daughter, who had such a mild reaction to it.
'Just what,' the King of Vraven thought slowly, 'did that fucker make my daughter see during the months he had her?'
Both arch priestesses watched the Primordial Villain fondle his governor inside a cathedral, and no amount of theological training had prepared either of them for this.
"What a weird creature you are, Quinlan Elysiar..." Velara whispered, her face begging for divine patience. "I'll never get used to you..."
Elisabeth did not share her endurance.
"Such depraved actions cannot be permitted!" She took a step forward, golden light flickering at her fingertips. "Villain! Release the buttocks of your woman at once, or I will-"
Velara caught her wrist. "Wait."
"What is it?! Can't you see the unforgivable sacrilege he's committing on sacred grounds-"
Velara studied the enforcer with scrutinizing eyes, then, having realized the truth, she whispered, "I had my suspicions but...You really don't know, do you?"
Elisabeth paused. Confusion crept into her expression beside the fury. "...Don't know what?"
Velara's grip softened, and the older priestess's gaze drifted back to Quinlan, who was now letting Jasmine guide him deeper into the cathedral while his hand remained exactly where it was.
"That man..." she said, and the weight in her voice stopped Elisabeth cold. "The Goddess gave me a task regarding him."
Elisabeth stared at her. "...A task?"

Velara nodded. Her voice was measured, the words polished by numerous sleepless hours of turning them over in her head. "The Goddess contacted me directly when this man conquered Whisperfield. She told me to find a path where the faithful could endure under his rule. To negotiate and cooperate rather than fight."

She glanced at Quinlan, who was listening to Jasmine somewhere deeper in the nave. "Her exact words regarding him were... 'The insufferable brat will no doubt be just that. You must remain strong, my herald. Endure his terrible attitude for the greater good.'"
"The Goddess..." Elisabeth's voice came out thin. "...called the Primordial Villain an insufferable brat?"

"She also said he is a conqueror, not a destroyer. The Goddess and that man have an arrangement. Political neutrality for us in exchange for our freedom to worship, heal, and operate without interference. He has honored every term so far."
"I see... That's why this church exists..." Alexios muttered, expression hard to read.
"???" The color drained from Elisabeth's face in stages, red to white to purple.
Her lips moved without sound, and the golden light that had been flickering at her fingertips sputtered once and died.
The Goddess had spoken. The Goddess had not only sanctioned the Villain's existence but even bid his followers to try cohabitation with him.
"Impossible..."
A sharp smack echoed through the nave, followed by a delighted yelp.
"Quin!" Jasmine's voice carried from deeper in the cathedral, more amused than scolding. "We're in a church! Control your urges..."
Elisabeth's head whipped toward the sound, and the sight of Jasmine looking up at Quinlan with a sly grin while rocking her hips once nearly broke her on the spot.
She turned back to Velara with desperation cracking through her voice. "But why didn't he tell me?! If the Goddess herself said as such, why didn't he say a single word?!"
Another smack rang off the cathedral walls. Jasmine giggled and shook her backside at him. "The first two were on the house, but the next one will cost you dearly, young man!"
"Sister." Felicity's voice cut through, gentle and honest. "You were screaming at him from the moment you saw him. You barely let him get a word in."
She tilted her head. "If he had claimed he had a deal with the Goddess, would you have listened? Or would you have screamed sacrilege even louder?"
Elisabeth opened her mouth. Closed it.
Felicity smiled, soft and sympathetic. "He knew it was pointless."
A third slap echoed through the holy chamber, crisp and shameless, and Jasmine's delighted laughter bounced off the vaulted ceiling. "Kya! Bad boy!"
Elisabeth's eyes rolled back and her knees buckled.
Alexios caught her under the arms before she hit the stone.

Quinlan and Jasmine returned from the nave at their own pace, the governor hugging his arm to her chest with both hands and leaning into his shoulder, her smile so content and her cheeks so flushed that she looked like a newlywed on her morning walk.
"Are we ready to proceed?" Quinlan asked, scanning the group. "Guess the Goddess didn't feel like speaking up herself."
"She rarely does... Every word costs her a lot," Velara admitted, voice small. "That was the first time the Goddess ever spoke to me in all my years of service."
"What a restricted existence she leads," Quinlan shook his head, knowing he would hate his life if he had to deal with so many headaches.
He'd have the urge to destroy all his restrictions and become free again.
"Or maybe you're just not important enough?" he asked Velara with far too much sincerity.
The Arch Priestess's forehead began bulging with a clearly visible vein. "My case is not an exception but the norm."
"Oh."
Velara's hands tightened into trembling fists. Why was that such a big surprise to him?!
His gaze next landed on Elisabeth, who was standing with glassy eyes, pale and unsteady.
He raised his palm, and compressed earth materialized above it, shaping itself into a clean, smooth jug in a single breath. A ribbon of water coiled from the air and filled it to the brim.
"Here." He held it out to her.
Elisabeth took the jug and drank in three long gulps without thinking, her throat working on instinct before her mind could catch up.

"!!" Then her eyes focused on the ceramic in her hands, and the color crashed back into her face as she realized she'd just accepted water from the Primordial Villain inside a cathedral and drained it like a woman lost in the desert.
Her face scrunched, but before she could do anything drastic, she froze with her cheeks full due to the two gazes that pressed into her back like a continent's worth of elven judgment.
Myrasyn and Isveth were watching her with smiles so sweet and eyes so dangerous that the message didn't need words.
Elisabeth swallowed.

"Ahem." Myrasyn then cleared her throat with impeccable delicacy, then blinked at Quinlan with wide, sparkling eyes that had absolutely no business being on a four-thousand-year-old queen. "Khm... Khm..."
Someone's throat seemed to be far too dry to even speak a single word...
Quinlan chuckled and shaped two more jugs from his palm, filling them the same way.
Myrasyn's eyes went wide as she received it, cradling the simple earthen cup to her chest with both hands as if he'd placed a sacred relic in her palms.
Beside her, Isveth clutched hers the same way, fingers curled tight around the rim, not daring to let a single drop escape.
Then they drank, and the way they did it made the entire cathedral go quiet.

Myrasyn brought the rim to her lips and took the smallest sip, her tongue meeting the water first, tasting it, savoring the nothing-special flavor of plain clean water as though it were the nectar of the First Tree itself.
Her ears twitched once, her lashes fluttered, and a soft hum left her throat before she tilted the cup for a second, longer sip. "How can it possibly be so delicious...?"
Isveth mirrored her queen one beat behind, her eyes closing as the water touched her lips, the tip of her tongue catching a drop that tried to escape down the rim. "I'm speechless..." she whispered.
"It's just water," Quinlan sighed.
"It's not!" the two protested without missing a beat.
Quinlan let it go and shaped one for all his guests.
Even Morgana was offered one.
The Queen of Vraven fixed him with an incredibly venomous glare, refusing to accept it.
Felicity looked at her mother, then shook her head with the long-suffering patience of a daughter who had stopped being surprised a long time ago. "Mom..."
Quinlan shrugged, drank the water himself, then turned back to Elisabeth.
"I owe you one more thing. Shall we?"
Elisabeth looked up at him, still flushed, still rattled, and the confusion that crept across her features was genuine. "...What?"

Confusion crept into her expression beside the fury.
"...Don't know what?"
Velara's grip softened, and the older priestess's gaze drifted back to Quinlan, who was now letting Jasmine guide him deeper into the cathedral while his hand remained exactly where it was.
"That man..." she said, and the weight in her voice stopped Elisabeth cold.
"The Goddess gave me a task regarding him."
Elisabeth stared at her.
"...A task?"
Velara nodded.
Her voice was measured, the words polished by numerous sleepless hours of turning them over in her head.
"The Goddess contacted me directly when this man conquered Whisperfield.
She told me to find a path where the faithful could endure under his rule.
To negotiate and cooperate rather than fight."
She glanced at Quinlan, who was listening to Jasmine somewhere deeper in the nave.
"Her exact words regarding him were... 'The insufferable brat will no doubt be just that.
You must remain strong, my herald.
Endure his terrible attitude for the greater good.'"
"The Goddess..." Elisabeth's voice came out thin.
"...called the Primordial Villain an insufferable brat?"
"She also said he is a conqueror, not a destroyer.
The Goddess and that man have an arrangement.
Political neutrality for us in exchange for our freedom to worship, heal, and operate without interference.
He has honored every term so far."
"I see...
That's why this church exists..." Alexios muttered, expression hard to read.
"???" The color drained from Elisabeth's face in stages, red to white to purple.
Her lips moved without sound, and the golden light that had been flickering at her fingertips sputtered once and died.
The Goddess had spoken.
The Goddess had not only sanctioned the Villain's existence but even bid his followers to try cohabitation with him.
"Impossible..."
A sharp smack echoed through the nave, followed by a delighted yelp.
"Quin!" Jasmine's voice carried from deeper in the cathedral, more amused than scolding.
"We're in a church!
Control your urges..."
Elisabeth's head whipped toward the sound, and the sight of Jasmine looking up at Quinlan with a sly grin while rocking her hips once nearly broke her on the spot.
She turned back to Velara with desperation cracking through her voice.
"But why didn't he tell me?!
If the Goddess herself said as such, why didn't he say a single word?!"
Another smack rang off the cathedral walls.
Jasmine giggled and shook her backside at him.
"The first two were on the house, but the next one will cost you dearly, young man!"
"Sister." Felicity's voice cut through, gentle and honest.
"You were screaming at him from the moment you saw him.
You barely let him get a word in."
She tilted her head.
"If he had claimed he had a deal with the Goddess, would you have listened?
Or would you have screamed sacrilege even louder?"
Elisabeth opened her mouth.
Closed it.
Felicity smiled, soft and sympathetic.
"He knew it was pointless."
A third slap echoed through the holy chamber, crisp and shameless, and Jasmine's delighted laughter bounced off the vaulted ceiling.
"Kya!
Bad boy!"
Elisabeth's eyes rolled back and her knees buckled.
Alexios caught her under the arms before she hit the stone.

Quinlan and Jasmine returned from the nave at their own pace, the governor hugging his arm to her chest with both hands and leaning into his shoulder, her smile so content and her cheeks so flushed that she looked like a newlywed on her morning walk.
"Are we ready to proceed?" Quinlan asked, scanning the group.
"Guess the Goddess didn't feel like speaking up herself."
"She rarely does...
Every word costs her a lot," Velara admitted, voice small.
"That was the first time the Goddess ever spoke to me in all my years of service."
"What a restricted existence she leads," Quinlan shook his head, knowing he would hate his life if he had to deal with so many headaches.
He'd have the urge to destroy all his restrictions and become free again.
"Or maybe you're just not important enough?" he asked Velara with far too much sincerity.
The Arch Priestess's forehead began bulging with a clearly visible vein.
"My case is not an exception but the norm."
"Oh."
Velara's hands tightened into trembling fists.
Why was that such a big surprise to him?!
His gaze next landed on Elisabeth, who was standing with glassy eyes, pale and unsteady.
He raised his palm, and compressed earth materialized above it, shaping itself into a clean, smooth jug in a single breath.
A ribbon of water coiled from the air and filled it to the brim.
"Here." He held it out to her.
Elisabeth took the jug and drank in three long gulps without thinking, her throat working on instinct before her mind could catch up.

"!!" Then her eyes focused on the ceramic in her hands, and the color crashed back into her face as she realized she'd just accepted water from the Primordial Villain inside a cathedral and drained it like a woman lost in the desert.
Her face scrunched, but before she could do anything drastic, she froze with her cheeks full due to the two gazes that pressed into her back like a continent's worth of elven judgment.
Myrasyn and Isveth were watching her with smiles so sweet and eyes so dangerous that the message didn't need words.
Elisabeth swallowed.
"Ahem." Myrasyn then cleared her throat with impeccable delicacy, then blinked at Quinlan with wide, sparkling eyes that had absolutely no business being on a four-thousand-year-old queen.
"Khm...
Khm..."
Someone's throat seemed to be far too dry to even speak a single word...
Quinlan chuckled and shaped two more jugs from his palm, filling them the same way.
Myrasyn's eyes went wide as she received it, cradling the simple earthen cup to her chest with both hands as if he'd placed a sacred relic in her palms.
Beside her, Isveth clutched hers the same way, fingers curled tight around the rim, not daring to let a single drop escape.
Then they drank, and the way they did it made the entire cathedral go quiet.

Myrasyn brought the rim to her lips and took the smallest sip, her tongue meeting the water first, tasting it, savoring the nothing-special flavor of plain clean water as though it were the nectar of the First Tree itself.
Her ears twitched once, her lashes fluttered, and a soft hum left her throat before she tilted the cup for a second, longer sip.
"How can it possibly be so delicious...?"
Isveth mirrored her queen one beat behind, her eyes closing as the water touched her lips, the tip of her tongue catching a drop that tried to escape down the rim.
"I'm speechless..." she whispered.
"It's just water," Quinlan sighed.
"It's not!" the two protested without missing a beat.
Quinlan let it go and shaped one for all his guests.
Even Morgana was offered one.
The Queen of Vraven fixed him with an incredibly venomous glare, refusing to accept it.
Felicity looked at her mother, then shook her head with the long-suffering patience of a daughter who had stopped being surprised a long time ago.
Quinlan shrugged, drank the water himself, then turned back to Elisabeth.
"I owe you one more thing.
Shall we?"
Elisabeth looked up at him, still flushed, still rattled, and the confusion that crept across her features was genuine.
"...What?"

chapters.title: Chapter 1777 Joyous Return
paragraphs: "I owe you one more thing. Shall we?"
Elisabeth looked up at him, still flushed, still rattled, and the confusion that crept across her features was genuine. "...What?"
Quinlan answered Elisabeth's question by tearing a hole in Velara's cathedral.
Wind gathered beneath the group in a single compressed column and lifted every person off the stone floor at once, smooth and effortless.
By the time Elisabeth realized her feet were no longer touching ground, the vaulted ceiling was already rushing toward them.
Quinlan raised one hand and the stone parted, folding outward in a clean circle to reveal winter sky.
The group floated through the opening into cold air above the city.
Velara, robes billowing around her ankles, watched her cathedral's roof peel apart and turned a look on Quinlan so dry it could have started a brushfire. "Are you doing this on purpose?"
She exhaled tiredly before he could respond. "Don't even answer. I know you are."
"Doing what on purpose?" Quinlan asked, the picture of innocence.
Velara's expression somehow found a way to go even drier.
She said nothing.
"I won't know what you mean if you don't tell me." The grin splitting Quinlan's face was the most satisfied expression he'd worn all day, and it told Velara everything his words denied.
Yes, he was doing all of this on purpose and he was having a great time while doing so.
"Villain!" Elisabeth's voice rose, but the heat cracked at the edges before it could truly build. The screeching that would've followed minutes ago came as uncertain and weak.

"To desecrate a holy sanctuary by..." She trailed off. The priestess who'd been hurling accusations all day had taken too many hits to her worldview to swing another, and she closed her mouth, visibly swallowing the lecture she'd been about to deliver.

The wind shifted and they shot across the rooftops fast enough that anyone on the streets below would've caught only a flicker against the winter clouds. Within seconds he set them down on a flat roof overlooking the city's main gate and the wide avenue leading up to it.
"[Warp Gate]." He flicked two fingers and the dimensional doorway bloomed open thirty meters past the city gate, its shimmering surface facing the settlement.
A soldier on the gatehouse wall spotted it first.
His spear tilted as he leaned forward, squinting, and then recognition hit and his whole face brightened.
"They're here!"
He grinned, grabbed the iron horn bolted to the wall, and blew three sharp notes into it. The signal rang across the district and bounced off heated stone.
After the first horn blow, the citizens froze.
"Invaders?!"

A woman clutching a bread basket stopped mid-step, a carpenter lowered his hammer, children paused their game to stare toward the gate, and for a breath the entire district held still because a horn from the walls meant visitors, and in a city this young, visitors could mean anything.
Then two more horn blows arrived, signaling a vastly different event than hostile invasion.

Just as the first figure stepped through the shimmer, a cry went up from the front of the crowd that had nothing to do with fear. "They're coming home!!" Children bolted toward the gate screaming for papa and mama, wives and husbands shoved past each other to get closer, and the street shattered into a stampede of joy.
The soldier who'd stepped through was blue-skinned, a man in his thirties, pale ghostly fire tracing his form, marking him as a creature no longer alive.
But his smile was.
"PAPA!!" A boy of five launched from the crowd and hit his legs so hard he stumbled, and the laugh that tore out of him as he scooped the boy up had nothing rehearsed in it.
More poured through.
Two boys sprinted past everyone and tackled a dead woman in partial armor who dropped to her knees and pulled them both in tight.
An elderly couple waited at the edge, unhurried, until their son walked to them and his mother pressed her forehead to his chest without a word.

A woman in an apron broke into a sprint and slammed into her dead husband hard enough to send them both staggering. "You're late," she managed with her face buried in his chest, voice cracking on the second word.
"The boss was ambushed by Elvardia. Had a lot to clean up."
"Hmph! Continental wars should know their place. You were helping me set the garden up and then you disappeared!"
"As I said-"
"I know, but I don't have to approve!"
"Let's go back to the garden, dear?"
"No, it's late now..." the woman pouted. Then she bit her lips. "Instead let's go to bed..."
"Say no more." The man lifted his wife and began hauling her back toward their new home.
The avenue filled with reunions too private to watch and too warm to look away from, laughter and crying tangled together in the winter air.

On the rooftop, Jasmine watched with quiet eyes and a smile she didn't need to brighten. Felicity stood beside her with both hands clasped at her chest, soft and warm, and Velara pressed her lips together and said nothing, all three quiet, because they'd seen this before and it still hadn't gotten old.

Alexios stood with his arms crossed, his expression giving away nothing, but his eyes tracked every reunion below. Beside him, Myrasyn's hand found Isveth's, and tears slipped down both elven faces in unison.
Morgana looked at her nails.
Elisabeth hadn't moved a single inch since the gate materialized.

"I promised I'd show you how my soldiers get to go home after being dismissed from duty." Quinlan's voice was low, meant for her alone. "I know you will argue it's staged. Smiles on puppets following my orders."

He tilted his head toward the avenue below. "So what do you propose? Should I have Kitsara disguise you tonight to help sneak into their homes and let you listen in to see how they live when they think nobody's watching? Or will that also not suffice?"
Elisabeth didn't answer.
Her gaze was on the avenue, where the dead were being hauled into homes by impatient wives and swarmed by children who refused to let go. They moved like people who'd been away too long.
Elisabeth's heart hammered against her ribs.

Her face cycled through a dozen expressions in the space of a few seconds, disbelief crumbling into confusion, confusion crumbling into nothing she had a word for, and her lips parted without producing sound.
Everything she'd been taught about the desecration of the dead, every sermon she'd delivered about the abomination of necromancy, was walking down the street below her being scolded about gardening.
Her hands trembled at her sides.
Elisabeth's knees hit the stone.
The Arch Priestess sank where she stood with her hands clasped before her chest, and the prayer that left her lips was so quiet it barely carried over the wind.
Tears streaked down her cheeks without ceremony, the thin silent kind that came when the truth of what she'd seen finally settled into place and there was nothing left to fight.
She prayed for a long time, and no one interrupted her.
When she finally looked up at Quinlan, her eyes were red-rimmed but clear.
Then...
Elisabeth bowed her head toward Quinlan from her knees.
"I apologize for my behavior." Her voice was thin and fragile, yet the sincerity in it was clear for all to hear.
"Your Fujimori woman was right." She raised her eyes again to meet his. "You're not a necromancer but the Necromancer. I understand now why the Goddess doesn't wish to eradicate your existence."
Felicity's smile could have lit the entire city.
Quinlan looked at the kneeling priestess for a long moment, and the surprise on his face gave way to real warmth. "Apology accepted."
Elisabeth smiled at that, soft and real. "Did my terrible behavior affect your opinion of the church?" she asked, worried.

chapters.title: Chapter 1778 The Most Infuriating Creature In Existence
paragraphs: Quinlan reached down and offered her his hand with the warmest, most open expression she'd ever seen on him, his entire face so friendly that the Primordial Villain could have passed for a priest handing out blessings. "No. Of course not."
Elisabeth's eyes lit up. She took his hand, let him pull her to her feet, and the relief that passed through her was the first real exhale she'd managed all day.
"After all," Quinlan continued, the extreme friendliness not shifting a single hair, "my opinion of your order has been rock bottom since long before I met you."
Elisabeth's grip froze.
"Hah?"
Her head tilted, her smile went sharp and dangerous, and golden light crackled through their joined hands hot enough that the air around their fingers shimmered.
Her voice was terrifyingly sweet. "Oh, is that so?"

Quinlan placed his free hand on top of her head and ruffled her hair with infuriating gentleness. "I'm glad we made up." He patted her head once more. "I really didn't want to have to enslave Felicity's sister too."
Behind them, Morgana's entire body went rigid.

Her neck strained sideways, veins bulging, jaw locked so tight her teeth could have cracked, because every fiber of the Queen of Vraven wanted to turn and incinerate the man who had just casually referenced enslaving her.
But Jasmine's earlier order hung over her like a leash, and Morgana's head refused to complete the turn no matter how hard she willed it.
She stood there, trembling with fury, neck twisted at an angle that would have concerned a physician, glaring at empty air three degrees to the left of Quinlan's face.
Meanwhile...
"Villain..."
The light blazed white.
Elisabeth's grip would have ground a lesser man's bones to powder, and her voice came out with a murderous calm that was worse than all of her screaming combined. "Remove. Your hand. From my head."
"Sure."
Quinlan removed his hand from her head and immediately, wind erupted beneath Elisabeth's feet and the Arch Priestess shot into the winter sky.
Her eyes narrowed into dangerous slits as she rocketed upward with her robes streaming behind her, and for a breathless moment she was nothing but a shrinking speck against the clouds.
Then she reached the peak of her ascent and began freefalling.
Her eyes burned with fury instead of fear, glaring down at the intolerable man.
Her hands were brought into prayer again, but the contents of this sermon were vastly different.
"O Goddess, your faithful servant calls upon your endless benevolence. I have devoted my life to your light. I have weathered heresy and hunted sinners without rest."

Her clasped hands tightened. "I beseech you, grant me strength. Strength that prevents me from wrapping my fingers around that infuriating man's throat and squeezing with otherworldly joy, for my patience has been spent in its entirety and my hands are dangerously available."

Quinlan didn't give her time to descend to the ground. Wind surged beneath the rooftop and the rest of the group rose with him as he shot forward across the city, carrying his guests in a current of compressed air.
Elisabeth was caught by the gust and fell in behind them, the expression on her face promising that the Primordial Villain would not live a long life.
"Sister!" Felicity drifted close in the airstream, beaming so brightly the sun felt redundant. "I'm proud of you! You apologized for your unruly behavior. That was really mature of you!"

Elisabeth's teeth clenched so hard her molars creaked. "Uttering those words in my moment of weakness is the biggest regret..." she ground out, every word dragged from her at knifepoint, "...of my life."
"Bleh!"
She stuck her tongue out at Quinlan's back with all the mocking spite her battered dignity could scrape together.
"Hehe! So cute!"
Felicity burst into merry giggles, floated closer, and placed her hand on top of Elisabeth's head, patting it with the exact same rhythm Quinlan had used.
"There, there..."
Elisabeth's face scrunched into a pout so fierce it could have ended many hearts.
Far below and several blocks behind, Arch Priestess Velara stood alone on the rooftop where he'd left her and watched Quinlan's rapidly receding back shrink into the winter sky.

"You motherfu-" She caught herself, pressed her lips shut, and exhaled through her nose. "You terrible spawn of the devil, you did not just leave me on a rooftop. Far from the Cathedral where I'm powerless. You simply wouldn't dare."
He would, and he did.
Velara reached into her pocket ring and pulled out the bolt of linen she'd purchased at the fabric stall.
She studied it for a moment then folded it into a neat square and pressed it to her face with both hands.
"MMMMRRRGGHH!!" She followed that up by screaming into it so hard her back arched.
She stomped her feet, threw punches at the Primordial Villain's distant silhouette, and kept going until her throat gave out. "Mmfgh... mmrrph...!!"
Then she pulled the linen away, smoothed her robes, tucked a loose strand behind her ear, and became the Arch Priestess of the Goddess once more.
She walked to the edge and lowered herself over it, and hundreds of years of reading scripture instead of climbing things made themselves violently apparent.
"Hyah?!"

Her fingers white-knuckled on the stone lip, her feet kicked at open air, and her robes snagged on a protruding nail and yanked taut, leaving the Arch Priestess suspended like laundry someone had forgotten to collect.

That was when gentle stairs of compressed earth began rising from the ground below, one step at a time, forming a clean staircase that ran up the side of the building and connected to the rooftop she had just climbed off of.
Velara watched them materialize from her dangling position, wide-eyed.
If she had waited ten more seconds, she could have walked down like a dignified servant of the Goddess. Instead, she was dangling from the rooftop.
The pocket ring was called upon again. The Cloth rematerialized. Delicate lips parted. The cloth entered again.
"MMMMRRRGGHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHH!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!"
The wind carried them south.
Quinlan flew at the front with Jasmine against his side while the guests trailed in the current behind them.
Elisabeth was still glaring at his back, Felicity was patting her sister's head between giggles, and the elves were quietly drying their tears.
Then a shape rose on the horizon, and every conversation died.
A new settlement's silhouette cut against the sky.
Then, as they descended toward the treeline, they spotted the first of its residents.
Children were playing in a forest clearing outside the walls.

A beastkin girl with dog ears, an elven girl with long pointed ears, a dwarven boy barely up to their waists, and two human children, all tangled together in some game that involved a lot of screaming and no discernible rules.
"This is!" Myrasyn's eyes went wide beneath her hood, the words dying before she could finish them. Isveth's hands flew to her mouth.
"Impossible..." Alexios whispered.
Quinlan and Jasmine exchanged a glance, eyes dancing, as they spoke in perfect sync:
"Dearest guests... We welcome you to our first settlement, named after the wonderful primordial Mearie, Miri Town."
It was time to show their guests just what was truly possible when the races weren't trying to kill each other on sight.
And then, it would be time to finally unearth what the Fujimori elders kept secret, Alexios had big decisions to make, and Quinlan...
It would finally be time for him to truly do as primordials do.

Her hands were brought into prayer again, but the contents of this sermon were vastly different.
"O Goddess, your faithful servant calls upon your endless benevolence.
I have devoted my life to your light.
I have weathered heresy and hunted sinners without rest."
Her clasped hands tightened.
"I beseech you, grant me strength.

Strength that prevents me from wrapping my fingers around that infuriating man's throat and squeezing with otherworldly joy, for my patience has been spent in its entirety and my hands are dangerously available."
Quinlan didn't give her time to descend to the ground.
Wind surged beneath the rooftop and the rest of the group rose with him as he shot forward across the city, carrying his guests in a current of compressed air.
Elisabeth was caught by the gust and fell in behind them, the expression on her face promising that the Primordial Villain would not live a long life.
"Sister!" Felicity drifted close in the airstream, beaming so brightly the sun felt redundant.
"I'm proud of you!
You apologized for your unruly behavior.
That was really mature of you!"
Elisabeth's teeth clenched so hard her molars creaked.
"Uttering those words in my moment of weakness is the biggest regret..." she ground out, every word dragged from her at knifepoint, "...of my life."
"Bleh!"
She stuck her tongue out at Quinlan's back with all the mocking spite her battered dignity could scrape together.
"Hehe!
So cute!"
Felicity burst into merry giggles, floated closer, and placed her hand on top of Elisabeth's head, patting it with the exact same rhythm Quinlan had used.
"There, there..."
Elisabeth's face scrunched into a pout so fierce it could have ended many hearts.
Far below and several blocks behind, Arch Priestess Velara stood alone on the rooftop where he'd left her and watched Quinlan's rapidly receding back shrink into the winter sky.
"You motherfu-" She caught herself, pressed her lips shut, and exhaled through her nose.
"You terrible spawn of the devil, you did not just leave me on a rooftop.
Far from the Cathedral where I'm powerless.
You simply wouldn't dare."
He would, and he did.
Velara reached into her pocket ring and pulled out the bolt of linen she'd purchased at the fabric stall.
She studied it for a moment then folded it into a neat square and pressed it to her face with both hands.
"MMMMRRRGGHH!!" She followed that up by screaming into it so hard her back arched.
She stomped her feet, threw punches at the Primordial Villain's distant silhouette, and kept going until her throat gave out.
"Mmfgh... mmrrph...!!"
Then she pulled the linen away, smoothed her robes, tucked a loose strand behind her ear, and became the Arch Priestess of the Goddess once more.
She walked to the edge and lowered herself over it, and hundreds of years of reading scripture instead of climbing things made themselves violently apparent.
"Hyah?!"

Her fingers white-knuckled on the stone lip, her feet kicked at open air, and her robes snagged on a protruding nail and yanked taut, leaving the Arch Priestess suspended like laundry someone had forgotten to collect.

That was when gentle stairs of compressed earth began rising from the ground below, one step at a time, forming a clean staircase that ran up the side of the building and connected to the rooftop she had just climbed off of.
Velara watched them materialize from her dangling position, wide-eyed.
If she had waited ten more seconds, she could have walked down like a dignified servant of the Goddess.
Instead, she was dangling from the rooftop.
The pocket ring was called upon again.
The Cloth rematerialized.
Delicate lips parted.
The cloth entered again.
"MMMMRRRGGHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHH!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!"
The wind carried them south.
Quinlan flew at the front with Jasmine against his side while the guests trailed in the current behind them.
Elisabeth was still glaring at his back, Felicity was patting her sister's head between giggles, and the elves were quietly drying their tears.
Then a shape rose on the horizon, and every conversation died.
A new settlement's silhouette cut against the sky.
Then, as they descended toward the treeline, they spotted the first of its residents.
Children were playing in a forest clearing outside the walls.

A beastkin girl with dog ears, an elven girl with long pointed ears, a dwarven boy barely up to their waists, and two human children, all tangled together in some game that involved a lot of screaming and no discernible rules.
"This is!" Myrasyn's eyes went wide beneath her hood, the words dying before she could finish them.
Isveth's hands flew to her mouth.
"Impossible..." Alexios whispered.
Quinlan and Jasmine exchanged a glance, eyes dancing, as they spoke in perfect sync:
"Dearest guests...
We welcome you to our first settlement, named after the wonderful primordial Mearie, Miri Town."
It was time to show their guests just what was truly possible when the races weren't trying to kill each other on sight.
And then, it would be time to finally unearth what the Fujimori elders kept secret, Alexios had big decisions to make, and Quinlan...
It would finally be time for him to truly do as primordials do.

chapters.title: Chapter 1779 Unruly Ruffians
paragraphs: Quinlan brought his guests down through the canopy before anyone on the ground could notice.

Wind cushioned each guest onto the broad limbs of an ancient oak overlooking the clearing, steady enough to stand on, and he threaded a current between the leaves that carried every sound from below to their ears as clearly as if they were standing in it.
Jasmine settled beside him and rested her cheek against his shoulder, watching the scene.
Below them, the children were close enough now to pick out faces, and the first thing that registered was the sound of one adult losing a battle she had no chance of winning.
A young woman in white nun's robes stood in the center of the clearing with her hands on her knees, bent double.

Her glasses had fogged and slipped halfway down her nose, freckles were flushed crimson across both cheeks, and her habit was streaked with so much dirt and grass that the white had become a suggestion.
"Come... back... here...!" she wheezed, reaching toward a dogkin girl who was already twenty meters away and accelerating.

"Catch me if you can, Sister Mira! The pack only follows the strong!" The girl's ears flattened with glee as she looped the clearing in three seconds, came sprinting past the nun close enough to ruffle her robes, and called "I can't bow to such a disappointment!" over her shoulder before she was gone again.
"You damned brat...!" Mira keeled over, nearly dying on the spot. "I don't want you to bow, just listen to your damned caretaker! I'm the adult and you're the child!"
"Such faulty logic won't work on me!" distant giggling was the response her grunts received.
"Goddess have mercy..." She braced her hands on her knees and breathed like a woman contemplating a career change.
Then she straightened, pushed her glasses up with the back of her wrist, and turned toward the tree where the elf girl had been sitting a few seconds ago.
The branch was empty.
"...Where did she go?"
A voice drifted down from considerably higher. "You look tired, Sister Mira. You should sit down and drink water. Lots of it."
The elf girl was perched on a branch twenty meters up, bare legs swinging, perfectly at ease, stroking the bark the way someone would pet a cat.
"Wah!" The nun was on the verge of suffering a heart attack.

Sister Mira, the freckled, bespectacled nun Quinlan had snatched off a rooftop during the siege of Greyhaven and dragged across the kingdom to help evacuate orphanages, had been calling him a motherfucker ever since.

Now, as a woman who only ever took care of human children up until a certain overly arrogant and unfairly handsome primordial scumbag brought her over to this accursed town, dealing with non-human kids was a whole new world, a world in which she was stumbling around with great difficulty...
"Come down from there this instant, young lady!" she screamed, though it sounded more pleading than threatening.
"I like it up here." Her pointed ears twitched, listening to something only she could hear. "Also, please lower your voice. You're disturbing mother nature."
The little girl began petting the tree as if consoling it. "Don't worry, the loud lady means no harm... She's just greatly misguided."
"I cannot believe this!" Mira muttered, fixing her glasses for what was clearly not the first time today, "Why won't you sit lower? What if you break your neck?"
"???" Pure confusion replaced the elf's expression, looking as if the mere idea of falling off a tree was alien to her.
"Haaah..." Mira gave up on the elf and spun around to find the dwarven boy, only to discover that the spot where he'd been standing was now an empty hole in the dirt.
"The depths are calling to me!" he shouted from below, his excited voice echoing.
"Oh no you don't!"
She dropped to her knees and plunged both arms in up to her elbows.
Her fingers found a boot and she pulled.
The boot came.
The boy did not.
"AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAARRRRRRRRRRRRRRGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGGHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHHH!"
She planted her feet and heaved, and the boy heaved right back.
"Unhand me, wench! I'm done living under the oppressive sun!"
The earth widened as he burrowed deeper with the stubborn efficiency of someone who was very good at this, and Mira's arms sank to her shoulders.
"You are not... a mole...!" she grunted, cheek pressed to dirt. "You are a child! Children do not live underground!"
A muffled voice rose from below. "Dwarves do!"
"You're SEVEN!"
The two human children sat on a log nearby, watching with the calm acceptance of being the only ones Sister Mira could actually catch.
"She's gonna lose," the boy said.
"She always does," the girl confirmed.
"The fresh meat... they're fun," the boy smirked, watching the nun's futile efforts.
"Super fun!" the girl cheered, feet dangling even faster with excitement.
In the oak above, nobody spoke.
Myrasyn's fingers had found Isveth's at some point during the chase and were gripping hard enough to tremble.
Her eyes moved from the dogkin girl still sprinting laps to the elf in the branches to the dwarven boy's hole, and each one pulled the same expression deeper across her face.
Alexios hadn't blinked in a while.
"Holy Son..." Myrasyn whispered, and the question had nothing to do with the game. "What's going on?"
"Absolute destruction," Quinlan grinned.
"That's not what I meant!" Myrasyn hissed, pouting. "The races! They're playing together!"
While 'playing together' might've been a bit of a stretch from a certain point of view considering each kid was doing their own thing, to Myrasyn, it was anything but a stretch.
They were all working together to have fun at the expense of their caretaker.
Such a scene had never been witnessed before. It was world-shattering.

"They're orphans of Miri Town, taken care of by the volunteer nuns and funded by us," Jasmine explained in Quinlan's stead seeing how he was content to keep their shell-shocked guests guessing. "The cruel nature of slavery left the non-human kids without parents while the human kids lost theirs to war, slavery, and other misfortune."
"Here she is."
"Our screeching superstar."
Voices drifted from the far side of the clearing.
Two women emerged from the path leading toward the settlement walls, each trailed by a cluster of children who poured from the treeline behind them like a dam had burst.
The first was an elven nun with ears every bit as long as Myrasyn's and a basket of bread on one hip.
Six children followed her in a loose pack: two elves, one dwarf, a human boy, and two beastkin who spotted the clearing's dogkin girl and broke into a sprint to join her with matching shrieks.
The second was a wolfkin sister with gray ears pressed flat beneath her wimple, carrying a blanket under one arm and a sack of bottles over the other.

Her group was the largest of the three, a dozen children, mostly human, with two dwarves, two elves, and a bearkin boy mixed in. They marched behind her in a neat line and scattered the instant they reached the clearing.
"Mira, people can hear you from the other side of the continent," the elf sister sighed.
"They just won't listen!" Mira shouted from the ground, still gripping the dwarf's boot with both hands. "Help me!"
The elf sighed, set down her basket, and looked up at the elf girl perched twenty meters above with extended arms.
"Come down."

chapters.title: Chapter 1780 Wimpy Nun
paragraphs: "Come down."
A calm, clear instruction.
The elf girl's ears perked.
She pushed off the branch and dropped straight into the elf sister's waiting arms.
"Yes, Sister!" She beamed, nuzzling into the nun's shoulder.
Mira stared.
Her eyes narrowed into slits so thin they could have cut glass. "She did it immediately," she whispered, her voice hollow. "I begged..."
The wolfkin sister cracked her neck, drew a slow breath, and opened her mouth.
"RETURN!" The snarl that came out shook the leaves off the nearest bush.
The dogkin girl froze mid-sprint on the far side of the clearing.
Her ears flattened, her tail tucked between her legs, and she came trotting back with her head low and sat on the blanket without a word.
Then the wolfkin turned toward the hole.

She dropped to all fours and dove in headfirst. The earth shook, a muffled shriek echoed from below, and the dwarven boy came flying out, dangling upside down by one ankle in the wolfkin sister's grip.
"Unacceptable!" he shrieked, swinging his fists at her arm. "This is tyranny! I demand a trial!"
"Eat first," the wolfkin said, and set him on the blanket.
She brushed dirt from her robes and turned to Mira, who hadn't moved from the grass.
"You're too nice to them," she said simply. "Assert yourself or these ruffians will never take you seriously."
Mira sat up slowly. Dirt caked her robes from collar to hem, grass stuck to her hair, and her glasses hung from one ear.
"Maybe..." She looked down at her hands. "Maybe a weak human woman like me just isn't cut out for this. I already struggled with human kids, but now..."
The words came out quiet, and the hurt in them was real.
She loved these children.
She wanted to be enough for them. And maybe she wasn't.
The clearing went still.
"Nonsense," the elf sister said firmly. "It has nothing to do with your race, physical strength, or gender."
The dogkin girl's ears drooped.
She crawled across the blanket to Mira's side and pressed against her arm.

"I'm sorry, Sister Mira..." Her voice was small. "I'll behave now... Please don't leave..." She curled tighter. "I was only messing with you because... because messing with Sister Mira is too much fun..."
The elf girl looked away.
She crossed her arms and lifted her chin.
"Sister Mira is a wimpy quitter," she told the tree she'd just climbed down from. "Hmph."
She did not look at Mira, yet her droopy ears gave her away.
The dwarven boy scoffed from where the wolfkin had deposited him. He crossed his arms and muttered at the ground.
"For a sun lover... she's not the worst."

Mira looked at the dogkin pressed against her arm, and the elf girl refusing to make eye contact, and the dwarf who had just delivered the highest compliment his seven-year-old dwarven heart could manage.
Her glasses fogged.
She pushed them up with the back of her wrist, and the smile that broke across her face was crooked and fragile and real.
"Let's eat, you damned brats."
The three nuns set up the meal with the practiced rhythm of women who did this every day.
The wolfkin sister spread blankets, the elf sister unpacked bread, cheese, dried fruit, smoked meat, bottles of milk, and a clay pot of stew that steamed in the cold air.
Mira sat with the dogkin girl still glued to her side and pretended her eyes weren't red.
The children converged in waves, running, walking, dropping from trees, crawling from holes. They arranged themselves on the blankets with the chaos of creatures who had done this a hundred times.
The elf girl took one look at the smoked meat and wrinkled her nose so hard her entire face compressed.
"That's a dead animal."
"It's delicious," the dwarven boy said, and took a bite large enough for three children while staring directly at her.
She turned away with her chin lifted and pointed ears twitching. "It's barbaric."
"More for me." He took a second piece. "Go munch on your leaves, there's plenty."
"Grr!!"
One of the newly arrived dwarven boys inspected the elf girl's pile of fruit and vegetables with open suspicion. "That's not food. That's what food eats."
"Your entire race lives in a hole!" one of the elves fired back.
"It's called a HALL, you uncultured swine!"
The dogkin girl dropped between the warring factions and ate everything within reach with undiscriminating joy, alternating between bread and meat and fruit without noticing that sides existed.
"See?" One of the elven girls pointed at the dogkin's meat-eating with vindicated horror. "Even she eats it!"
"She eats everything," the dwarven boy said, with more respect than judgment. "Yesterday she ate a pinecone."
"It looked tasty!" the dogkin girl protested, ears flattening.
"Did you finish it after realizing it wasn't?"
"...Maybe."
Above them, the silence had changed.
Myrasyn was watching an elven girl break off a piece of bread and hand it to the dwarven boy because his hands were full of meat and he couldn't reach.
He thanked her with his mouth full.
She wrinkled her nose at the crumbs but didn't pull away.
Her throat worked once.
What she was watching didn't exist on the continent.
Not in any living memory, not in four thousand years of history.
Elven children did not share food with dwarven children while a wolfkin poured them milk.
The suggestion alone would have drawn silence in any court.
Three nuns in white robes were managing it between meals, and the hardest part of their afternoon was extracting a seven-year-old dwarf from the ground.
Alexios's hand had found the branch beneath him at some point, and his knuckles were white around it.
"This isn't staged," he said, and the words came out rough.
Elisabeth stood on her branch with her arms at her sides, watching a human nun, an elven nun, and a wolfkin nun care for orphans of every race as if it were the most natural thing in the world.

Sister Mira scolded the dwarven boy for eating too fast while wiping crumbs from his cheeks with her sleeve, and the elf sister was handing bread to a dogkin child, and none of them treated any of it as remarkable.
Her hand found the Goddess's sigil at her throat. The brightness in her eyes had nothing to do with anger.
Felicity was gripping her branch with both hands, leaning so far forward that Alexios had to catch her shoulder. "So cute!! Can we join them? I'm really hungry..."
"No," Alexios said simply.
"Why not?" Quinlan grinned, fully embracing the fun uncle role.
Alexios turned to look at him with narrowed eyes. Before he could voice his opinion, however, wind swept them off the tree.

"Learn to live, old man," Quinlan's voice carried through the gust toward the ancient king just before Quinlan landed in the clearing first, and every child within thirty meters went silent. "Aren't you gonna keel over and die any moment now?"
A beat passed.
Then the dwarven boy pointed. "THE DARK KNIGHT!!"
The clearing erupted.
Boys shot to their feet and charged, questions tumbling over each other before they'd taken three steps.
The girls froze, hands flying to their hair frantically to ensure all was in order and their postures straightening in a wave that rippled across the blankets.
The wolfkin sister's nose twitched.
She sniffed the air twice, and her ears pinned back. "How... I didn't sense..."
The elf sister's head snapped toward the canopy, eyes widening as two immense elven presences flooded her senses, suppressed until this moment. "They suppressed my detection..."
Mira was on her feet before anyone else moved.

Her glasses sat crooked, her robes were still caked in dirt, and the look on her face when she recognized who was standing in her clearing went from shock to fury so fast it skipped everything in between.
"You!" She jabbed a finger at him. "What do you want now?! Haven't you done enough tormenting me?!"
"Sister Mira!!!" the girls yelped in sync. "You're talking to..."
"I know who I'm talking to! That's my problem!" Mira growled.
Indeed, the overly expressive nun had been through a few adventures with Quinlan, such as being dropped from the skies and only caught with her face inches from the ground.
"Can we join?" Quinlan asked, nonchalantly ignoring the screeching

"It's barbaric."
"More for me." He took a second piece.
"Go munch on your leaves, there's plenty."
"Grr!!"
One of the newly arrived dwarven boys inspected the elf girl's pile of fruit and vegetables with open suspicion.
"That's not food.
That's what food eats."
"Your entire race lives in a hole!" one of the elves fired back.
"It's called a HALL, you uncultured swine!"
The dogkin girl dropped between the warring factions and ate everything within reach with undiscriminating joy, alternating between bread and meat and fruit without noticing that sides existed.
"See?" One of the elven girls pointed at the dogkin's meat-eating with vindicated horror.
"Even she eats it!"
"She eats everything," the dwarven boy said, with more respect than judgment.
"Yesterday she ate a pinecone."
"It looked tasty!" the dogkin girl protested, ears flattening.
"Did you finish it after realizing it wasn't?"
"...Maybe."
Above them, the silence had changed.
Myrasyn was watching an elven girl break off a piece of bread and hand it to the dwarven boy because his hands were full of meat and he couldn't reach.
He thanked her with his mouth full.
She wrinkled her nose at the crumbs but didn't pull away.
Her throat worked once.
What she was watching didn't exist on the continent.
Not in any living memory, not in four thousand years of history.
Elven children did not share food with dwarven children while a wolfkin poured them milk.
The suggestion alone would have drawn silence in any court.
Three nuns in white robes were managing it between meals, and the hardest part of their afternoon was extracting a seven-year-old dwarf from the ground.
Alexios's hand had found the branch beneath him at some point, and his knuckles were white around it.
"This isn't staged," he said, and the words came out rough.
Elisabeth stood on her branch with her arms at her sides, watching a human nun, an elven nun, and a wolfkin nun care for orphans of every race as if it were the most natural thing in the world.

Sister Mira scolded the dwarven boy for eating too fast while wiping crumbs from his cheeks with her sleeve, and the elf sister was handing bread to a dogkin child, and none of them treated any of it as remarkable.
Her hand found the Goddess's sigil at her throat.
The brightness in her eyes had nothing to do with anger.
Felicity was gripping her branch with both hands, leaning so far forward that Alexios had to catch her shoulder.
"So cute!!
Can we join them?
I'm really hungry..."
"No," Alexios said simply.
"Why not?" Quinlan grinned, fully embracing the fun uncle role.
Alexios turned to look at him with narrowed eyes.
Before he could voice his opinion, however, wind swept them off the tree.
"Learn to live, old man," Quinlan's voice carried through the gust toward the ancient king just before Quinlan landed in the clearing first, and every child within thirty meters went silent.
"Aren't you gonna keel over and die any moment now?"
A beat passed.
Then the dwarven boy pointed.
"THE DARK KNIGHT!!"
The clearing erupted.
Boys shot to their feet and charged, questions tumbling over each other before they'd taken three steps.
The girls froze, hands flying to their hair frantically to ensure all was in order and their postures straightening in a wave that rippled across the blankets.
The wolfkin sister's nose twitched.
She sniffed the air twice, and her ears pinned back.
"How...
I didn't sense..."
The elf sister's head snapped toward the canopy, eyes widening as two immense elven presences flooded her senses, suppressed until this moment.
"They suppressed my detection..."
Mira was on her feet before anyone else moved.

Her glasses sat crooked, her robes were still caked in dirt, and the look on her face when she recognized who was standing in her clearing went from shock to fury so fast it skipped everything in between.
"You!" She jabbed a finger at him.
"What do you want now?!
Haven't you done enough tormenting me?!"
"Sister Mira!!!" the girls yelped in sync.
"You're talking to..."
"I know who I'm talking to!
That's my problem!" Mira growled.
Indeed, the overly expressive nun had been through a few adventures with Quinlan, such as being dropped from the skies and only caught with her face inches from the ground.
